source_text: Εἶτ᾿ ἐπεὶ πολλάκις ὀνομάζει κρύφιον τὸ δόγμα, καὶ ἐν τούτῳ αὐτὸν ἐλεγκτέον, σχεδὸν παντὸς τοῦ κόσμου ἐγνωκότος τὸ κήρυγμα Χριστιανῶν μᾶλλον ἢ τὰ τοῖς φιλοσόφοις ἀρέσκοντα. τίνα γὰρ λανθάνει ἡ ἐκ παρθένου γέννησις Ἰησοῦ καὶ ὁ ἐσταυρωμένος καὶ ἡ παρὰ πολλοῖς πεπιστευμένη ἀνάστασις αὐτοῦ καὶ ἡ καταγγελλομένη κρίσις, κολάζουσα μὲν κατ᾿ ἀξίαν τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας γέρως δ᾿ ἀξιοῦσα τοὺς δικαίους; ἀλλὰ καὶ μὴ νοηθὲν τὸ περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως μυστήριον θρυλεῖται γελώμενον ὑπὸ τῶν ἀπίστων. ἐπὶ τούτοις οὖν λέγειν κρύφιον εἶναι τὸ δόγμα πάνυ ἐστὶν ἄτοπον· τὸ δ᾿ εἶναί τινα οἷον μετὰ τὰ ἐξωτερικὰ, μὴ εἰς τοὺς πολλοὺς φθάνοντα, οὐ μόνου ἴδιον τοῦ Χριστιανῶν λόγου ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ τοῦ φιλοσόφων, παρ᾿ οἷς τινες μὲν ἦσαν ἐξωτερικοὶ λόγοι ἕτεροι δὲ ἐσωτερικοί· καί τινες μὲν ἀκούοντες Πυθαγόρου, ὡς „αὐτὸς ἔφα,“ ἄλλοι δ᾿ ἐν ἀποῤῥήτῳ διδασκόμενοι μενοι τὰ μὴ ἄξια φθάνειν εἰς ἀκοὰς βεβήλους καὶ μηδέπω κεκαθαρμένας. καὶ πάντα δὲ τὰ πανταχοῦ μυστήρια κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα καὶ τὴν βάρβαρον κρύφια ὄντα οὐ διαβέβληται· διόπερ μάτην μηδὲ νοήσας ἀκριβῶς τὸ κρύφιον τοῦ χριστιανισμοῦ διαβάλλει αὐτό.
pass_a_gloss: Since he often names the doctrine secret, and in this he is to be reproved, since almost the whole world has known the proclamation of Christians rather than the things pleasing to philosophers. For what escapes notice is the birth of Jesus from a virgin and the crucified one and the resurrection of him believed by many and the judgment announced, punishing indeed the sinners according to worth but highly valuing the righteous? But also the mystery of the resurrection, not understood, is ridiculed by the unbelievers. Therefore to say that the doctrine is secret is very absurd; that there is something like an inner truth, not reaching the many, is not unique to the Christian speech but also of the philosophers, among whom some were outer speeches and others inner; and some hearing Pythagoras, as 'he himself said', others being taught in secret things not worthy to reach the ears of the profane and not yet purified. And all the mysteries everywhere, according to Greece and barbarian lands, being secret are not despised; therefore in vain, not having understood accurately the secret of Christianity, he slanders it.

pass_b_english: Since Celsus repeatedly calls the Christian doctrine "secret," he deserves reproof on this point, because almost the whole world knows the Christian proclamation better than the teachings that please philosophers. After all, what escapes notice? The birth of Jesus from a virgin, his crucifixion, his resurrection believed by many, and the announced judgment that punishes sinners as they deserve while highly honoring the righteous? Even the mystery of the resurrection, though not understood, is ridiculed by unbelievers. So to claim the doctrine is secret is very absurd.

The idea that there is something like an inner truth that does not reach the many is not unique to Christian teaching; philosophers have it too. Among them some gave outer discourses and others inner ones: some heard Pythagoras only as "he himself said," while others were taught in secret things not worthy to reach the ears of the profane and not yet purified. And all the mysteries everywhere, in Greece and among barbarian lands, though secret, are not despised. Therefore, without accurately understanding the secret of Christianity, Celsus slanders it in vain.

review.notes: Checked all clauses in paragraph 1. Pass A and Pass B both accurately reflect the Greek text. Pass B provides a more fluent rendering of the causal relations (e.g., 'he deserves reproof on this point' for 'ἐν τούτῳ αὐτὸν ἐλεγκτέον') without adding external meaning. Scripture references are not present in the Greek source, so none were required. The title 'Christian Doctrine Not Secret' accurately captures the thought of the passage.
